title: Compassion, Part 2: Contemplation of Death
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett invites the community to explore their fear of abandonment as a practice, acknowledging its prevalence and potential for growth. They then shift focus to Joan Casey's passing, using her presence as an opportunity to come together with the Shambhala Center and cultivate compassion through contemplation of death and impermanence. By exploring these themes, Nomon hopes to inspire listeners to develop greater emotional awareness, acceptance, and connection to their own lives and the lives of those around them.

sentences.text: I'm really glad you're here.
I've been noticing lately that there's a lot of, maybe you have this too, a lot of fear of abandonment.
Do you have that fear?
You just have this feeling like everybody's going to leave.
So it's just part of our makeup, I guess.
Something to practice with.
And you don't have to come later and help me with it.
Just being here is perfect.

I wanted to mention that a wonderful friend of our sangha, of all the sanghas in Bellingham, from the beginning of sanghas in Bellingham, which is not such a long history, a 25-year history or something like that, a woman named Joan Casey, died yesterday morning.
Wonderful person.
She was 75.
She'd have been 76 in two weeks.

I never quite got the medical details right, but her husband, John Watts, is a blogger, and apparently if you read his blog you can find out the medical details and lots of other lovely things too, I'm sure.
Bellingham something?
**Participant:** Hamster.
Bellinghamster.
I think it's just hamster.
Bellinghamster.
I don't know what it is.
Bellinghamster.
Bellinghamster.
Bellinghamster.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
So you can read about Joan on the Bellinghamster blog.
A pulmonary crash of some kind.
I didn't see Joan Casey often, but I always enjoyed her bright spirit so much when I did.
The last time I saw her was at a screening of the film *States of Grace* at the Pickford.
*States of Grace* is an amazing thing too.
It's a very intimate documentary about the very long recovery of a woman named Grace Daman, who was in a terrible car crash on the Golden Gate Bridge in California.
Grace was a resident of Green Gulch Farm Zen Center, and has been for many, many years, and was when I was there as a young man.
So I knew Grace a little, and Grace was there for the screening of this film about her life.
I still don't understand it.
I talked to her about this, and I talked to the filmmaker, who was also there.
Frank, I forget his last name.

Can you imagine having a horrific car crash that everybody expects you won't survive, and then this incredibly challenging recovery, and you have a teenage daughter with disabilities and all the stuff that would go with that, and then you invite this camera crew to live with you and document the whole thing, including documenting when you have fights with your ex-partner in the middle of all this?
It's an amazingly intimate and real film, unbelievable.
You should see this film, *States of Grace*.
Grace is the name of the woman who was hurt.
It's about her and her partner, Fu Schroeder, who's a Zen teacher.
Anyway, Joan was there at the screening, and it's the kind of thing where there's lots of hanging out in the lobby before and after.

Somehow Joan Casey knew everybody in that lobby, and she appears in front of you like, "Oh, Joan, how good to see you," and you have this very bright, very brief conversation, and suddenly she's not there anymore and she's talking to somebody else.
That's what she was like, in a wonderful way.
And she was that way with all the sanghas in Bellingham.
She'd appear and disappear.
I don't know that she's been to a formal Zen practice in 10 years at least, but to me she feels like part of the sangha.
I remember when we were remodeling this place eight or nine years ago, something like that, she came and went a fair amount then.
You'd see her here, at some of the work parties.
She'd come, not exactly work, but she'd show up and do this kind of thing, and you felt very good that she had come.
And then it was all over, and our original budget was $10,000 and we had spent more than $30,000 and we couldn't quite afford it.
We were trying to buy the heating panels.
I don't know if you noticed these white panels.
They're so subtle and silent.
They're the perfect heating for a meditation hall.
And we only had enough to buy about half the number that the heating guy recommended, something like that.
Somehow Joan appeared at that moment and said, "Oh, I'll write you a check."
So that's why we have a full complement of heating panels.
I'm grateful to Joan for that, among many other things.
Joan was a serious student of Dzogchen Buddhism, the Tibetan, intensive meditation style of Buddhism.
She went back and forth all the time between their home in San Francisco, and maybe they had a place in Sausalito too.
It's not clear to me all the things that she did in her Dzogchen sanghas in Sausalito, California.
So she would go back and forth, and it was on their way back that she suddenly took ill and was hospitalized in Redding, California, and died there.
So we'll have a memorial for Joan in Bellingham.
It turned out Joan also always knew what she wanted, so she left detailed instructions with her husband about what kind of memorials she should have.
She wanted memorial services with the Zen community and with the Bellingham Shambhala Center community.
I talked it over with Jenny Warwick, the teacher of the Shambhala Center.
We all agree that Joan wouldn't mind if we combine those two, because so many people knew her, and how would they choose which one to go to?
We just started the conversation today about this.
She just died yesterday.
But I hope in the last week of April, probably at the Shambhala Center because they have a bigger room, we'll have a memorial.
So whether you remember Joan Casey or not, I hope you'll come.
It's a wonderful opportunity to celebrate the deeper quality of the Bellingham Buddhist sanghas.
And if we do it at the Shambhala Center, it's a great excuse to finally get over there and check it out, if you haven't yet.
I think it's funny.
When we first started the original Dharma Hall in 1991, Joan was quite involved in that.
The groups were very small and we were all meeting in living rooms.
One of our first meeting places was the fireplace room at Fairhaven Library.
We were in a little teeny room for a while, and then we were meeting in a therapist's group room.
Anyway, we banded together in 1991 to form Bellingham Dharma Hall in a building on Unity Street.
One of the things we thought is that we would all be like Joan.
We would all flit around and go to all the different sanghas and learn all these four different traditions: Soto Zen, Thich Nhat Hanh style mindfulness, Vipassana and Shambhala.
But the reality is we're busy enough and work hard enough that one evening is enough.
So it didn't really happen so much.
Joan was one of the few people who really dipped in and experienced all the sanghas.
And to this day, 1991, 25 years later, is that true?
Yes, 25 years later, I have only once been to a Shambhala Center service, and that was for a funeral also.
So if you haven't been to the Shambhala Center, don't feel bad.
We know you're not sectarian.
You just are too busy.
So this may be Joan's way.
Since this was Joan's way of living, maybe it'll inspire all of us to band together with the Shambhala Center.
I know many people from the Bellingham Insight Vipassana Sangha hope to come too.
So we'll let you know on the email when and where.
And of course, I wish I knew Joan better.

There should be a word for the particular kind of melancholy feeling you get, that feeling of wishing you'd spent more time with somebody, that appears the moment, the instant, you find out that they've died.
Have you had this feeling?
I bet in Japanese they have a word for that.
Anyway, I have that feeling.
And it's painful too, because it's like the fiction that you're going to get around to it, get around to seeing that person more, getting around to getting to know them.
Joan was very welcoming.
You called her up and hung out at her house any time.
She probably would have given you lots of gifts and stuff too.
But I never got around to it.
So when they die, that fiction that you'll get around to it later just comes crashing down, doesn't it?
During our service just now, I put Joan's name card on the central altar, so she's right in front of Buddha.
We were bowing to her and chanting with her, and later we'll do a formal memorial that names her in the dedication.
As you know, I've been trying to understand a little more about compassion.
I've always loved the groundedness and the wisdom emphasis in Zen.

But a little like Norman has done, my teacher Norman Fischer, our guiding teacher, with his study of the Tibetan mind training slogans called Lojong and his great book he made about those talks, called *Training in Compassion*, I've realized that I'm a little low on emotional awareness, emotional intelligence and compassion.
Maybe it's a pretty common thing, just like not going to the other sanghas.
Maybe we're all a little low on these things.
I love people a lot, actually, but I don't really communicate that very well.
And left to my own devices, I get a little bit self-focused.
Maybe a lot self-focused.

So I've been trying to study Tibetan Buddhist teachings on compassion, because for whatever reason, Tibetan Buddhism explicated compassion as a system of training, as far as I know, better than any system of spirituality in the world.
Whether that really showed up in feudal Tibetan society, I'm not so sure.

But the teachings and the practices are there, and the practitioners who are supported to practice them deeply are certainly amazingly warm and compassionate, surviving stuff like long imprisonment and torture with good grace.
Anyway, I've been reading some of the Tibetan materials and trying to make sense of them.
It's fairly dense.
And I've also been studying secular adaptations of these Tibetan wisdom teachings, with a good bit of psychology and poetry and common sense wisdom thrown in.
In the last talk I gave in this seat, I talked a little bit about the first step in Tibetan compassion training.
The first step is the deep realization and the continued practice of an important thought: that all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering.
Of course that's obvious, duh.
Like most spiritual teachings, duh.
That's probably the real smell test for a good spiritual teaching.
When you hear it, your first response should be, "Oh yeah."
And your second response should be, "Oh, I don't really live that way.
I don't really know that in a deep way.
I don't live as if I really knew that."
We don't live as if we really knew that all beings want happiness and freedom from suffering.
I think that was a little scattered talk, but I think it's on the website.
You can listen if you like, or just study that yourself, even better.
The second step, at least in the particular book that I've been studying, a book by Jeffrey Hopkins, I forgot to bring it.
I forgot the title.
*Training in Compassion* or something, compassion.
He was a longtime translator of His Holiness the Dalai Lama.
Western guy, Jeffrey Hopkins, scholar.
It's actually a fairly poor book.
I don't recommend the book, just to save you the trouble.
I'm going to try to make sense of it.
I can just hang out and listen.
I don't get it.
Maybe it's because he's a translator.
I mean, it's wonderful that he made the book.
I don't mean to sound disparaging, because that's obviously not very compassionate.
But objectively speaking, it's not the best book, and it's hard to read.
It's like he's writing in back-translated Tibetan or something like that.
There are lots of fragments.
But it's a beautiful thing that it exists, and it's a way of accessing a very deep tradition.
So I'm grateful that he wrote this book.
Anyway, what he suggests as one of the next steps after deeply contemplating that thought is very topical to where I started our talk.
The second step is to contemplate death, which is not the first thing you think about when you think about compassion and love.
And this is not unique to the Tibetans.
The contemplation of death, and death and death, is a core Buddhist practice in all Buddhism, and probably all religious systems, all philosophical systems.
It's what mortal people can't avoid, right?
And they suffer if they do, and they live limited, stilted lives if they try to avoid deeply contemplating death.
In the mindfulness sutta from early Buddhism, there's a very long section, a very detailed section about how you should go to the charnel grounds.
They had open cemeteries, and they didn't bury people in those days, I guess.
They would be cremated or just put somewhere, I guess.
And there are detailed instructions for how to go in there and meditate while looking at corpses.
It was a stepwise process of picking corpses in different stages of decomposition very deliberately.
So you should read this, actually.
I don't know that any modern teachers of the mindfulness sutta really quite teach that part.
We're a little low on corpses, I guess.
Not that we're low on death, though.
We're just good at hiding it.
So it's not just the Tibetans.
Sometimes I've offered people the suggestion of a wonderful practice, which is maybe our version of the charnel ground practice: go to the graveyard.
Go to the cemetery.
Go to Bayview Cemetery, and just walk and stand and breathe.
You can read some of the gravestones and wonder about the people's lives.
That's sort of the story of death.
More importantly, go to just be with death, to feel death.
We're blessed to have many people in the sangha who work in the hospice centers and work with people who are close to the end of life.
So we have a lot of good teachers here about this.
Different branches of Buddhism have different ways of talking about this, different ways of remembering that life is short and life is precious.
Within the Buddhist system of many different kinds of worlds and different kinds of rebirths, it's seen as especially remarkable that we're in a human form right now.
It could have been any number of other kinds of forms.
Of course we take that a bit for granted, don't we?
We're not always too excited about being a human.
It seems like a pain sometimes.
But in the face of death, it becomes a little more precious.
The core teaching in all of Buddhism is: death is certain.
Only the time of death is uncertain.
That's the only thing we don't know.
Death is certain.
Nothing much else is certain, you know?
That's the one thing.
The Tibetans have a set of four thoughts that are designed to inspire us turning towards practice, and in these four thoughts is the reality of death.
Here's one of many versions.
*The freedoms and opportunities of this life are extremely difficult to attain.
Being impermanent, all things must die.
Virtuous and harmful actions cause their inevitable results.
The nature of samsara is suffering.*
So this is a motivational phrase, contemplating how rare it is to have a human body, how certain death is, and how what we choose to do actually really does matter.
Virtuous and harmful actions cause results.

And the nature of our limited view of life, which they call samsara, and we'll talk about that word later, the nature of a limited view of life, a life that denies this reality of death and cause and effect and the preciousness of our human life, the nature of that life, no matter what you do, is suffering.
So anything other than deeply practicing is a kind of Titanic deck chairs kind of deal.
Another version, found in an early Buddhist text called the Upajatana Sutta, has a list of five instead of four.
Here's Thich Nhat Hanh's version of the five remembrances of early Buddhism, the five remembrances.
This is what I was chanting that one time when I was practicing at Bayview Cemetery, walking around chanting this.
Not this exact version.
*I am of the nature to grow old.
There is no way to escape growing old.
I am of the nature to have ill health.
There is no way to escape ill health.
I am of the nature to die.
There is no way to escape death.
All that is dear to me and everyone I love are subject to change.
There is no way to escape being separated from them.
My actions are my only true belongings.
I cannot escape the consequences of my actions.
My actions are the ground upon which I stand.*
Many of our wonderful Zen stories, the pithy Zen stories called koans, are about the intimacy of life and death.
They're not so far apart, not so separate.
Here's one of many.
This one happens to feature the same Chinese Zen master Yun Men whom I mentioned in the last talk.
Remember the one about why do you put on the nine panel robe when you hear the sound of the bell?
This one's very short.
That one was short too, another two-liner.
A monk asked Yun Men, "How is it when the tree withers and the leaves fall?"
A monk asked Yun Men, "How is it when the tree withers and the leaves fall?"
Yun Men replied, "Body exposed in the golden wind."
"Body exposed in the golden wind."
This has a certain feel to it, doesn't it?
Exposed in the golden wind.
These stories get misunderstood as puzzles because of the nature of our mind, right?
We want to figure that out.
Like, was that a reference to something?
Is the Golden West probably an ancient Chinese story?
I've got to look this up.
And that probably is true.

But we can also read these with an eye towards the feeling of connection and intimacy between withering and falling, between being willing to be exposed to the golden wind, between intimacy and life and death.
So we don't have to figure them out if we don't want to.
We can just feel them.
How is it when the tree dies?
How is it when we die?
Are we gone?
I talked to Jon Watts, Jon's husband, on the phone this morning, just the day after she had died.
Your wife of, I don't know, many decades, I don't know how long they were married, 25, 30 years minimum.
And the very next day he's driving home, he pulled over to talk to me.
And I said what you say, right: "So sorry, sad, sad news."
And he said, "I am sad, but it's okay.
Her spirit is flying.
It's flying now."
I don't think he has a literal idea of some white stuff that's flying around that's called the spirit.
It's a little more like this.
He knows that the body is exposed in the golden wind.
He knows somehow, on his first day of bereavement, that it's horrible, it's so sad, and it's beautiful.
Golden.
I was really moved that he could say that.
He wasn't just trying to cheer me up or get me off the phone, or not start crying.
I think he was really being very honest.
I think the actual words he said were something like, "It's sad, but it's okay.
Her spirit is flying far and wide."
When people go, we all wake up a little, don't we?
We pay a little more attention.
We realize we haven't been paying so much attention until that moment.
I was listening a little bit to a Dharma talk by one of our Zen teacher colleagues in Portland.
I don't know if you know this, but Portland is like a Buddhist Mecca.
There are many, many, many Buddhist groups there, and two of the largest Soto Zen groups in the country, and maybe the planet, are in Portland.
You think New York, San Francisco, but Portland gets overlooked, maybe because it's so weird.
But anyway, a significant death in the Zen community there happened two years ago.

The Dharma Rain Zen community, which is the larger, I think, of the two by a good bit, is a very rich and intimate Zen community, which we could talk about at length, and you should visit them sometime, Dharma Rain Zen community in Portland.
It was founded by a couple who trained in Shasta Abbey, and so we studied in our practice period about their teacher, Jiyu-Kennett Roshi.
They went by their Dharma names.
Kyogen was the man of the couple, and Gyokuko was the woman.
Kyogen was walking down the hall one day after breakfast in 2014.
I remember when it was: it was at sesshin in Indianola in September.
He had a massive heart attack and died on the spot, just like that.
Somehow, when I was looking around a little bit on the internet thinking about this talk, I encountered some wisdom from Gyokuko, a Dharma talk by her that was given three weeks after Kyogen died.
For all of its incredible ability to distract us, the internet is really pretty wonderful too.
So we should remember to use the internet in a wonderful way.
I was just looking for one of those other koans about death, and I couldn't remember which case it was, and I was Googling it, and there was this talk by Gyokuko, and I know her as well.
She said in this talk, she's talking about Kyogen not being there.
She's talking to her community three weeks after he died, and she said, and another bereaved person, you know, this is her husband who died: "Who are you without that voice?"
So think of someone you've lost.
Who are you without that voice?
Without that face?
Without that person?
Without that mirror reflecting you back to you?
"Who are you without that?
We've set out on a journey," she said to them.
"We are three weeks into this journey.
And I would encourage you not to be in a hurry.
Don't be in a hurry to get remade.
Don't be in a hurry to stop being undone.
This is a precious journey full of possibilities.
It may be useful for you to relax around this and accept.
Just as you didn't choose this time to undergo this journey, you also don't get to choose what you experience along the way.
You can relax about that.
You can choose to turn towards it.
You can choose to experience it completely."
I have no doubt that's how she was practicing with this incredible loss.
She was speaking to people like her who deeply loved Kyogen, and he was a really lovely guy.
Like, one of the most lovable Zen teachers you ever could have met.
Zen teachers aren't always notably lovable, you know?
They are, but sometimes you have to kind of find it.
But you'd meet him and in five minutes you'd fall in love.
And he could be strong, of course, and clear, but very lovable.
Then she quoted Kyogen.
She quoted somebody sending her a condolence note quoting Kyogen about something important Kyogen had said to this student: "For a long time the grief is the most underappreciated of human emotions.
Most people avoid looking at it and they miss so much."
So it's not that appreciation of death is something that we can learn so that we can endure death, so that we can handle death.
Appreciation of death is a condition that supports the practice of softening into compassion.
And it seems like true compassion requires that we become undone.
We don't choose the journey into compassion, it seems.
But it's a precious journey full of possibilities.
So it's useful for us to know that we can relax and accept whatever life we have, and whomever we get to have it with, because we won't have them long.
So I want to close with a poem.
This is a mysterious poem because I literally found this in my pocket today.
I don't have an idea how it got there, but I'll leave it at that.
It's a poem called "Walking Meditation on a Quest for Peace and Finding Joy."
The scene you have to set for yourself is walking the kind of Vipassana, or we do it in mindfulness classes, style walking, where you walk back and forth outside.
So picture this on a big lawn.
*A universe lives in ten feet of grass.
Joy strewn along a narrow path.
Tiny creatures go about their day.
Grass is growing every which way.
A speck of dew glistens in the sun.
A treat for my longing heart.
It winks at me, beckoning me to stay.
Its sparkle touches my soul.
And then again, sprouted up, a gift from spring, a daisy roots his home.
Fresh white, whiter than white.
A yellow center, a tribute to the morning sun.
A dandelion, a weed yet full of life.
A comfort to a passing bee.
The wind, it vibrates the tallow grass, just a tickle for my anticipating mind.
Clumps of dead grass decaying, nourishment for the eternal universe of a ten foot patch of grass.*
So thank you very much for listening and for being here and for continuing to practice.
